strengths: Simple and elegant hardware design: The system achieves hyperspectral imaging using only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, making it highly practical, cost-effective, and easy to replicate compared to systems requiring custom DOEs or complex coded apertures.

Efficient and mathematically sound reconstruction: By exploiting the low-rank statistics of natural spectra and the Block Circulant with Circulant Blocks (BCCB) structure of the forward model, the authors derive a fast matrix inversion for plug-and-play ADMM. This allows sub-second reconstruction (< 0.64s), which is orders of magnitude faster than conventional optimization methods.

Strong experimental validation: The proposed method outperforms several state-of-the-art baselines (both optimization-based and learning-based) in synthetic benchmarks, achieving superior PSNR and SSIM, while exhibiting robustness against spectral hallucinations.

Real-world prototype demonstration: The authors built a physical prototype and validated its capability on real scenes under challenging low-light conditions (25 lux), showing high-fidelity spectral reconstruction.
weaknesses: Temporal capture constraint: Because the system relies on physically translating a lens to capture a focal stack of N images (typically 5 to 10), it is inherently restricted to static scenes. This limits its applicability to dynamic real-world scenarios compared to snapshot spectral imagers.

Strict assumptions on scene depth and FOV: The forward model assumes the target lies within a flat, narrow depth of field (34 cm) and close to the optical axis. Unmodeled aberrations like spherical aberration, lateral chromatic aberration, and defocus of out-of-DoF objects require center-cropping and limit the operating volume of the camera.

Sensitivity to calibration and mechanical wear: The reconstruction quality heavily depends on precise calibration of the spectrally varying PSFs across different lens positions. Over time, mechanical wear or shift in the actuator's precision could degrade performance.

strengths: Simple and Cost-Effective Hardware: The system uses only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, avoiding expensive custom diffractive optical elements (DOEs), liquid crystal tunable filters, or coded apertures.

Excellent Computational Efficiency: By leveraging low-rank eigenspace projection and the Block Circulant with Circulant Blocks (BCCB) structure for fast matrix inversion within a plug-and-play ADMM framework, the reconstruction takes less than a second (0.64s). This is orders of magnitude faster than traditional optimization-based computational imaging methods.
High Photon Efficiency: The design avoids light-blocking elements like coded apertures or narrow spectral filters, making it highly effective under low-light conditions.

Mitigation of Hallucinations: Unlike pure data-driven approaches that can hallucinate spectral features, the physics-based forward model ensures high spectral accuracy, as demonstrated by the metamerism experiment in Figure 3.
Solid Hardware Validation: The authors built a physical prototype and quantitatively evaluated it on a Macbeth color chart, demonstrating strong performance in real-world settings.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to Scene Depth: The forward model assumes the scene lies within a narrow, predetermined depth of field (34 cm at 2.8 m). For scenes with significant depth variations, depth-induced defocus will mix with chromatic defocus, degrading reconstruction quality.
Limited Field of View (FoV): To avoid unmodeled off-axis aberrations (e.g., lateral chromatic aberration and spherical aberration), the images must be center-cropped, restricting the effective FoV.

Susceptibility to Motion Artifacts: Because the focal stack is captured sequentially by translating a lens, the system is limited to static scenes. Any movement during the sweep will introduce spatial-spectral artifacts.

strengths: The proposed optical design is simple, elegant, and highly cost-effective, utilizing only two off-the-shelf lenses and a standard grayscale sensor, avoiding expensive custom diffractive optics or bulky prisms.

The physics-based optimization algorithm (PnP-ADMM combined with eigenspace projection and BCCB fast matrix inversion) is well-formulated, allowing for very fast (< 1 second) reconstruction while avoiding the hallucination artifacts common in end-to-end data-driven methods.
The paper provides a comprehensive evaluation including both rigorous simulations with realistic noise models and a real physical prototype, showing clear improvements over existing baseline methods.
The demonstration of metamer detection (distinguishing real vs. fake food) successfully showcases the practical utility of the recovered spectral information.
weaknesses: The system has a strict requirement that the target scene must be within a narrow, pre-calibrated depth of field (34 cm in the experiments). For scenes with significant depth variations, depth-induced defocus will be conflated with chromatic defocus, leading to severe reconstruction errors.

Because the system requires physical translation of a lens to capture multiple frames sequentially, it is not a snapshot system. This makes it highly susceptible to motion blur and restricts its applicability to strictly static scenes.

The practical field of view (FoV) is highly limited; as noted by the authors, they had to center-crop the images to avoid unmodeled off-axis aberrations such as lateral chromatic aberration and spherical aberration.

The spectral resolution is inherently limited by the broad-band nature of the chromatic defocus PSFs, which might smooth out fine spectral features or sharp absorption peaks compared to scanning spectrometers.

strengths: The optical design is exceptionally simple and elegant, leveraging the natural chromatic aberration of two off-the-shelf refractive lenses rather than relying on expensive custom diffractive optical elements (DOEs) or complex coded aperture masks.

The proposed reconstruction algorithm is highly efficient and robust. By projecting the spectra onto a PCA eigenspace and utilizing Block Circulant with Circulant Blocks (BCCB) properties for fast matrix inversion in the frequency domain, it achieves sub-second reconstruction times while maintaining physical interpretability and avoiding deep-learning hallucinations.
The paper is exceptionally well-written, with highly clear explanations of the forward model, system calibration, and optimization steps.

Extensive experiments in both simulation and on a real hardware prototype validate the method. The paper demonstrates outstanding performance compared to eight state-of-the-art computational spectral imaging modalities, particularly showing high robustness in low-exposure conditions.
The real-world prototype results on the Macbeth color chart and diverse natural scenes demonstrate impressive spatial and spectral fidelity.
weaknesses: Since the system requires physical translation of a lens across five discrete positions to capture the focal stack, it is inherently limited to static or slow-moving scenes. While the paper acknowledges this limitation, the mechanical transition time between shots could be more clearly specified.

The calibration process is quite elaborate, requiring a narrow-band liquid crystal tunable filter (LCTF) to measure the point spread functions (PSFs) across wavelengths and lens positions, which might hinder easy replication by researchers without specialized optical hardware.

The working depth range is relatively narrow (34 cm in the prototype). Scenes with large depth variations will suffer from depth-dependent defocus that deviates from the calibration model, which could degrade the spectral reconstruction accuracy.

strengths: Extremely simple, low-cost, and compact optical design using only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor, which preserves high photon efficiency by avoiding light-blocking filters or apertures.

Highly efficient and fast reconstruction algorithm (<1 second) leveraging a Plug-and-Play ADMM framework with eigenspace projection and fast Block Circulant with Circulant Blocks (BCCB) matrix inversions.
Robust performance under low-exposure/low-light scenarios where the high photon throughput of the system provides a significant advantage over dispersive and filter-based alternatives.

Solid experimental validation consisting of comprehensive simulations (on KAIST and CAVE datasets) and real-world experiments on a physical hardware prototype, achieving state-of-the-art results in PSNR and SSIM.
weaknesses: The multi-shot nature of the acquisition (translating the moving lens to 5 discrete positions) restricts the system to static or slow-moving scenes, limiting its applicability for dynamic hyperspectral imaging.

The system is constrained by a narrow depth of field working range (34 cm) to prevent depth defocus from being confounded with chromatic defocus, which restricts the depth variations allowed in target scenes.

Reconstruction quality is highly dependent on precise calibration of the point spread functions (PSFs); minor depth variations or mechanical calibration drifts can introduce spatial or spectral artifacts.

strengths: The hardware design is highly practical, cost-effective, and elegant, requiring only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor rather than expensive custom-fabricated diffractive optical elements (DOEs) or complex coded apertures.

The reconstruction algorithm is exceptionally fast, achieving sub-second (<1s) runtime. This is a massive improvement over traditional optimization-based or deep-learning reconstruction methods that often take minutes.

The paper provides a comprehensive and thorough evaluation, comparing the proposed method against eight state-of-the-art computational spectral imaging systems in both simulation and real-world experiments.
A physical hardware prototype was successfully constructed and calibrated, demonstrating high-quality spectral and spatial reconstructions of real-world scenes and targets.
weaknesses: The system has a severe limitation regarding scene depth (depth-spectral ambiguity). Since it relies on defocus to encode spectral information, the forward model assumes a flat scene at a fixed distance (2.8m within a 34cm working range). Real-world 3D scenes with varying depths would corrupt the spectral recovery due to depth defocus.

As a multi-shot system requiring the sequential capture of 5 frames with physical lens translation, the method is limited to static scenes and is highly vulnerable to motion artifacts during the capture sequence.

The core optical concept of using longitudinal chromatic aberration and focal sweeping for spectral estimation is conceptually incremental, as similar ideas have been explored in prior work (e.g., spectral focal sweep or bio-inspired chromatic blur vision).

Crucial technical details, specifically the exact derivation of the fast BCCB-based matrix inversion that enables the sub-second speedup, are relegated to the supplementary material, making the computational contribution of the main text feel somewhat incomplete.
